To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) We present the first fully distributed, low-constant approximation algorithms for the MPS problems for standard metrics in low-dimensional spaces, and (2) We present the best known approximation algorithms for the LCC clustering problem and the lowest-id clustering problem in ad-hoc mobile networks.

(i) we present a general framework for efficient approximation algorithms for the MPS with update time O(1), (ii) we present a family of distributed approximation algorithms for the L1, L2, and L∞ MPS problems with update time O(log n) and constant approximation factors, and (iii) we formally analyze two well-known ad-hoc network clustering algorithms.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: Given a set of mobile objects, how can we efficiently approximate their maximum coverage with a minimum set of fixed objects (piercers)?
the following question: How can we adapt to the mobility of nodes in a distributed manner, and maintain a low approximation factor for the mobile piercing problem?
a problem that is both of theoretical interest, and has direct applications to clustering in ad-hoc and sensor networks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the mobile piercing set framework provides a simple, general and efficient tool for the design of distributed and decentralized approximation algorithms for the MPS problems for standard metrics in low dimensional vector spaces, and can also be directly applied to the design of distributed clustering algorithms for ad-hoc networks.

the proposed framework provides a unified and simple way to obtain efficient and fully-distributed algorithms that adapt to the mobility of objects in the plane, for the mobile piercing problem on unit disks and nonuniform disks, and for the mobile k-center and k-median problems.
we provide efficient and fully decentralized algorithms that can be used to provide theoretical analyses of popular 1-hop cluster algorithms in mobile ad-hoc networks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, for the first time, we provide theoretical performance guarantees for the LCC algorithm, and for the first time provide approximation algorithms for the MPS with constant update times for nonuniform disks, for the L2 metric on two- and on three- dimensions.
we have provided a general framework for obtaining constant-factor approximation algorithms, with low update time, for the MPS problem for a wide variety of metrics and space dimensions.
we provide a general framework for obtaining low-constant approximations for a wide class of metrics in low-dimensional spaces and for nonuniform disks.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the mobile piercing set can be efficiently approximated for standard metrics, and can be used as a building block for the efficient design of distributed and decentralized approximation algorithms for a number of problems of practical significance in ad-hoc and sensor networks, including 1-hop clustering and data dissemination.
the proposed framework for approximating the MPS problem can be directly adapted to provide theoretical performance guarantees for clustering algorithms in ad hoc networks.
the mobile piercing set framework is a simple, general and effective tool for obtaining approximation algorithms with low update times for the clustering problem in ad-hoc wireless networks.
